content.title: About
content.content: Coconut water is the clear liquid found inside young green coconuts. The sweetened version contains added sugar or another sweetener, making it taste sweeter and more palatable. It is rich in electrolytes such as potassium, sodium, and magnesium, and is often used as a natural sports drink.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Coconut water naturally contains fewer calories than most fruit juices.
Sweetened versions often use cane sugar or fruit syrup to preserve the coconut’s natural flavor.
It is considered a “natural” isotonic drink because of its high potassium content.
In some countries coconut water is sold as a concentrate that is diluted with water before consumption.
A single coconut palm can produce up to 50 liters of water per year.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: A rich electrolyte profile helps replenish fluids lost during exercise.

items.title: Heart support
items.content: Potassium contributes to normal blood pressure and heart function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Coconut water contains virtually no fat, making it a light beverage.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: It provides vitamin C and small amounts of phenolic compounds that combat free radicals.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: A modest amount of dietary fiber can support regular bowel movements.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The sweetened version may contain significant added sugar, which is undesirable for people with diabetes or those watching their weight.

items.title: Coconut allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to coconut products.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Some commercial products can have elevated sodium, which should be considered by those with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Coconut water can be enjoyed chilled as a refreshing drink, used in smoothies, cocktails, or in cooking as a substitute for water or fruit juice. The sweetened version is often served after workouts for quick energy replenishment.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened packages in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, keep refrigerated and consume within 3–5 days.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-vegetab.title: Egg Omelet with Vegetables (No Added Fat)

content.title: About
content.content: An egg omelet with fresh vegetables (excluding dark‑green leafy vegetables and tomatoes) prepared without added fat. Eggs provide high‑quality protein, B‑vitamins, and minerals, while the vegetables add fiber, vitamins, and antioxidants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are one of the most affordable sources of complete protein.
Cooking without added oil retains most of the nutrients in the omelet.
Vegetables such as bell pepper, onion, carrot, and zucchini are rich in vitamins C and A.
The lack of added fat reduces the calorie count, making it suitable for weight control.
Gentle cooking over low heat yields a softer, more tender texture.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Eggs contain all essential amino acids, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs are high in B12, riboflavin (B2), and folate, important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Fiber and micronutrients from vegetables
items.content: The added vegetables provide dietary fiber, vitamin C, vitamin A (beta‑carotene), and potassium, beneficial for heart health and immunity.

items.title: Low calorie density
items.content: Absence of added fat makes the dish lower in calories, useful for diet‑focused eating.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Vitamins C and A from the vegetables help neutralize free radicals and support eye health.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg proteins.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked eggs can harbor Salmonella; ensure the omelet is fully cooked.

items.title: Excluded vegetables
items.content: Dark‑green leafy vegetables and tomatoes are omitted because they can increase acidity and affect flavor without added fat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beat the eggs, stir in finely chopped vegetables (bell pepper, onion, carrot, zucchini), season with salt and pepper. Pour the mixture onto a dry non‑stick pan, cook over medium heat, gently lifting the edges until the omelet sets but remains soft inside.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The omelet is best enjoyed fresh. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat in a pan without adding oil.

content.title: About
content.content: Greens is a blend of frozen leafy vegetables (spinach, broccoli, kale, green peas) that have been blanched and have added plant fat to improve flavor and texture. The product is ready to eat after heating and is ideal for quick meal preparation.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The mix contains at least five different leafy vegetables, providing a broad spectrum of nutrients.
Added fat enhances absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.
Freezing preserves most vitamins and minerals, comparable to fresh vegetables.
Often used in fast‑food kitchens and ready‑meal production to save time.
Greens can be stored in the freezer for up to 12 months without quality loss.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains vitamin A and carotenoids
items.content: Support vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Phytonutrients
items.content: Antioxidants such as lutein and zeaxanthin protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Fat improves nutrient absorption
items.content: The added plant fat helps the body better absorb fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: Allergy to plant oils
items.content: The product may contain soy or sunflower oil, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Some versions are lightly salted; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Leafy greens can contain oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat Greens in the microwave or skillet for 3–5 minutes, add to soups, stews, pasta, or use as a base for vegetable patties. Enhance with spices, soy sauce, or cheese for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen at –18 °C in the original packaging. Once thawed, consume within 24 hours and do not refreeze.

content.title: About
content.content: Oatmeal (regular or quick‑cooking) is prepared with water and added fat. Oats (Avena sativa) are a cereal grain cultivated in temperate regions. The flakes have a mild, slightly nutty flavor and a hearty texture that retains much of the grain’s fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oats are among the oldest cultivated crops, with evidence of use dating back over 5,000 years in Mesopotamia.
Quick‑cooking oats are pre‑steamed and cut thinner, which speeds up hydration.
Oats contain beta‑glucan, a soluble fiber known to help lower cholesterol levels.
In traditional Scottish cuisine, oats are used to make “porridge,” a thick stew of oats cooked in water or milk.
Oats are frequently used as a base for plant‑based milks and vegetarian burger patties.

items.title: Rich in beta‑glucan
items.content: Beta‑glucan helps reduce LDL cholesterol and supports healthy gut microbiota.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates provide sustained energy and help maintain stable blood glucose levels.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: Iron is essential for hemoglobin formation, while magnesium supports muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Low in sugar
items.content: Prepared with water and no added sugar, oatmeal fits well into low‑sugar diets.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: The combination of fiber, antioxidants, and healthy fats contributes to heart health.

items.title: Oat allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to oats or oat proteins.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can bind minerals and reduce their absorption; soaking or sprouting lowers its level.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Oats are often processed on the same equipment as wheat, so people with celiac disease should choose certified gluten‑free oats.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Oatmeal can be cooked as a hot porridge, blended into smoothies, used in baked goods, energy bars, or as a base for vegan “meat” alternatives. Adding a small amount of fat (butter, oil, cream) enhances flavor and improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store oatmeal in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation.
